introduction: This guide follows one picture through the writings: the Messenger of God as a sun. The readings kept here say that the sun is one though it dawns from many points, that its seasons return, that its rays cannot be accepted while the sun is refused, that most people were veiled when it rose, that its light continues after its setting, and that those who turn to it are asked to become lamps and stars in their turn. The picture is very old and widely shared, so the quotations set beside the readings come from the Psalms and the prophets, the Gospel of John, the Qur’an, Plato, the Upanishads and the Gita, and from poets who looked at the sun and at the dark. Most of them stand alongside; some doubt, with the Preacher, Kant or Emerson, whether a returning sun brings anything new or whether a person needs any light but their own.
questions: The readings say the sun is one though its dawning-points are many. What does that picture ask of someone who honours one Messenger and not another?
Several readings say that the sun’s changes are really changes in us. Where have you found that a change you blamed on the times was a change in where you stood?
Why, in the readings and in John’s Gospel, do people turn away when the light appears? Which of the reasons given seems truest to you?
After the sun has set, the readings say, its rays continue. How does a community tell the difference between living by those rays and mourning a light it thinks is gone?
Kant and Emerson trust the light within a person; the Buddha asks his followers to be lamps to themselves. What can that light do, and what do the readings say it cannot?
The last readings ask people to be lamps and stars. What would it mean this week to give light without wanting to be looked at?

outside.why: Plato too reaches for the sun when he wants to say what the highest reality does: it lets things be seen and lets them grow.
The Sermon on the Mount gives the same charge to its hearers: the light is to be seen in what a person does.
The psalmist already calls God a sun, and in the same breath a shield: light and warmth, and shelter too.
The last of the Hebrew prophets promises a sun of righteousness that heals and makes the young grow, as this reading says of the Center of illumination.
Francis praises the visible sun as a brother who bears a likeness of the Most High. Does loving the outward sun help a person to understand the inward one?
The sun that rises on East and West alike is the Gospel's picture of a love that makes no distinction among people.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of Christ as the brightness of God's glory, which is the reading's own argument about the sun and its rays.
The psalm also takes the outward heavens as a sign: what the eye sees there is telling of something that the eye cannot see.
The Preacher watches the same sun rise and set and finds only weariness in it. What makes one person see sameness and another see renewal in a returning sun?
A bishop of the third century uses the picture for the church: many rays, one light. The reading uses it for the Messengers themselves.
The Persian poet says of the prophets what this reading says: the lamps differ, and the light in them is one.
The Qur’an sets the sun's steady course among the signs of God; the Báb draws on that same sign for the one who returns.
Genesis says the lights of heaven were set there for signs and for seasons, which is how the Báb reads the sun's rising.
The Qur’an says the sun and moon were given measured stages so that people could reckon time; the reading reckons spiritual time in the same way.
The promise after the flood is that the seasons will not cease. The reading says the same of the seasons of the spirit.
Isaiah looks to a day when the sun will never set again. The reading says the Sun of Reality will rise and set for ever. Can both hopes be held together?
The creed of the fourth century speaks of light from light to say how what comes from God is not other than God.
James calls God the Father of lights, in whom nothing varies or turns: the source gives because of what it is.
Tennyson calls our systems of thought broken lights of something greater than they. Is a mirror's share of the sun a loss, or all that a mirror could ever want?
The Gospel distinguishes in the same way: John the Baptist was sent to bear witness to the light and was not himself that light.
The old book speaks as everyone then spoke, of a sun that moves and can be made to halt. What changes when we learn that the motion is ours?
The Qur’an tells how the sun looked to a traveller at the edge of the world: a description of how things appear from where the traveller stands.
The first letter of John says that in God there is no darkness at all; whatever darkness there is belongs to where we are walking.
In Genesis the greater light is made to rule the day and give light upon the earth: its whole purpose there is the earth's good.
Pope finds one power warming in the sun and living in everything. Does that leave room for the reading's sharp difference between a living sun and a dead earth?
The Gospel adds the other half: light needs an eye, and if the eye is unsound the whole body is dark. What keeps an eye sound?
Socrates is accused of holding, with Anaxagoras, that the sun is only stone. Does knowing what the sun is made of take anything from what it may stand for?
Jesus answers Philip in the same terms: whoever has seen him has seen the Father, and the two cannot be taken apart.
The Gita can only say that a thousand suns rising at once might resemble that glory: no light of human making comes near it.
The Buddha's last counsel is that his followers be lamps to themselves. The reading says a lamp is not enough. What can a person's own light do, and where does it stop?
John's Gospel opens with the same sorrowful observation: the light shines, and the darkness does not take it in.
The Qur’an speaks of those who would put out God's light with their mouths, and says that the light is perfected all the same.
The Gospel gives a reason for the veil: people prefer darkness when their own deeds would not bear the light.
He came to his own and his own did not receive him: John says of Christ what this reading says of those who see the Sun and deny it.
Shakespeare's king describes what sunrise does to those who worked in the dark: their deeds stand bare and they tremble at themselves.
Plato's prisoners, used to shadows, find the light painful and turn on the one who brings word of it.
The first words spoken in Genesis are a command for light, and the darkness gives way at once, as in this reading.
Thoreau says that light which puts out our eyes is darkness to us, and that a day dawns only for those awake. What does being awake to a sunrise ask?
The Qur’an pictures unbelief as layer upon layer of darkness, in which a man can hardly see his own hand.
For Kant the darkness is of our own making and the way out is the courage to use our own understanding. Is that courage opposed to the sunrise in this reading, or needed in order to face it?
Jesus tells his disciples that his going away is for their good, since what he sends afterwards will remain with them.
The disciples stood gazing up after a cloud took Jesus from their sight, and were told not to stand gazing.
Tennyson gives the plain human side of such a loss: longing for a hand that is gone and a voice that is still.
In John's Gospel Jesus warns that the light is present only a little while and that darkness follows. How does that warning sit beside the reading's assurance that the rays have not declined?
The sonnet knows a sun that shone for one hour and was then masked by cloud, and refuses to think the less of it.
Longfellow's well-known line says it simply: behind the clouds the sun is still shining.
Paul writes of a light that shines in human hearts and is seen in a face, which is what this reading longs to behold.
Micah speaks for anyone in hard times: when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light to me.
FitzGerald's Omar opens with the sun scattering the stars before it; beside that light the lesser ones do not count.
Emerson complains that people speak of revelation as something long ago given and done, as if God were dead. Is mourning a sun that has set a way of making that mistake?
The Qur’an describes the Hour with the same signs that this reading recalls: the sun overthrown and the stars falling.
In Exodus the people are led through the wilderness by fire that gives them light by night.
John's Gospel says the same of Christ: the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we beheld his glory.
In Joseph's dream the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him: the story this reading draws upon.
Blake says that if the doors of perception were cleansed, everything would appear as it is. Who removes the veil: the flame, or the one who looks?
In Acts a light shines in the prison where Peter lies chained, and the chains fall from his hands.
A poet imprisoned in the seventeenth century wrote that stone walls do not make a prison for a mind that is free.
Isaiah's words are among the best known in scripture: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Emerson tells each person to watch the gleam of light that flashes across the mind from within rather than the brightness of sages. What does that inner gleam need a sun for?
Jesus makes the claim in the present tense as this reading does: I am the light of the world.
Isaiah calls on his hearers to arise and shine because their light has come; the announcement is also a summons.
Habakkuk joins the same two pictures, glory and the sea: the earth is to be filled as the waters cover the sea.
John of Patmos sees a figure whose face is like the sun shining in its strength.
Zechariah's song in Luke calls the one who is coming the dayspring from on high, who gives light to those who sit in darkness.
The second letter of Peter speaks of a day-star that rises in the heart, after a lamp that shone in a dark place.
The Qur’an foretells a day when the earth will shine with the light of her Lord.
The psalm hears the heavens speaking day and night, in a language that needs no words and reaches every land.
Dante begins his Paradise with the glory that shines through the whole universe, more in one place and less in another.
Abraham in the Qur’an turns from star, moon and sun because each one sets. What would a sun that is always dawning ask of the one who loves it?
Even the Preacher, who doubts so much, says that light is sweet and that it is pleasant for the eyes to behold the sun.
Blake asks whether the divine countenance ever shone upon his own clouded hills: the question of a people waiting.
John's Gospel calls it the true light, which gives light to every person who comes into the world.
The Gospel says the coming will be like lightning that comes out of the east and shines as far as the west.
The prayer of the Upanishad is a seeker's prayer in its shortest form: lead me from darkness to light.
Kipling's verses speak for the confidence the reading describes, a West sure that it must teach the East. What does a sun that rises in the East say to that confidence?
The psalm says of the sun that it goes from one end of heaven to the other, and nothing is hidden from its heat.
The Qur’an says of God that He brings those who believe out of darkness into light.
Hosea says the Lord's going forth is as sure as the morning, and that He comes like rain upon the earth.
The ancient blessing of the priests asks for the same thing: that the Lord make His face shine upon you.
Milton, blind, addresses the light itself and asks whether he may speak of it without blame.
The Light Verse of the Qur’an is the source of this prayer's picture: a lamp within a glass, the glass like a shining star.
The first letter of Peter also speaks of a people chosen and called out of darkness into a marvellous light.
Paine mocks the person who prays as though to change God's mind. What is being asked for in a prayer like this one, if it is not that?
Many ask who will show them any good; the psalmist asks only for the light of God's countenance.
The psalmist finds strength in the same place: the Lord is my light, so whom shall I fear?
Paul calls his readers to wake because the night is far spent and the day is at hand.
The psalm calls on the sun, the moon and every star of light to give praise; thanksgiving here is the whole creation's work.
Proverbs compares the path of the just to the light of dawn, which shines more and more until the full day.
The psalm joins the same two pictures as the reading, the spring and the light: with Thee is the fountain of life, and in Thy light we see light.
Jesus uses the picture of a vine and its branches for the same dependence: the branch lives by what it is joined to.
Jesus says to his followers that they are the light of the world, and that a lamp is not lit to be hidden.
Hopkins, seeing everything else in leaf, ends his poem with a plea to be made to grow: send my roots rain.
The letter to the Ephesians says: you were once darkness, but now you are light; walk as children of light.
Portia, coming home at night, notices how far one small candle throws its beams, and likens it to a good deed.
Blake's child is taught that we are placed on earth for a little while so as to learn to bear the beams of love. Is being educated by a sun something to be borne as well as enjoyed?
Paul tells the Thessalonians that they are children of the day, and so should keep awake and sober.
Paul hopes the Philippians will shine as lights in the world, in the middle of a crooked generation.
Daniel promises that the wise, and those who turn many to righteousness, will shine like the stars for ever.
Jesus says of John the Baptist that he was a burning and a shining light: one person kindled by another greater than he.
Wordsworth pictures the soul as a star that had its setting elsewhere and arrives here from afar. Does hardship dim the radiance a person came with, or bring it out?

psalm-tabernacle-for-the-sun.text: In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun, Which is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race. His going forth is from the end of the heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it: and there is nothing hid from the heat thereof

john-i-am-the-light-of-the-world.text: Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life

revelation-countenance-as-the-sun.text: And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength

revelation-no-need-of-the-sun.text: And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof. And the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it: and the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honour into it

isaiah-sun-shall-no-more-go-down.text: The sun shall be no more thy light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light unto thee: but the Lord shall be unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory. Thy sun shall no more go down; neither shall thy moon withdraw itself: for the Lord shall be thine everlasting light, and the days of thy mourning shall be ended

luke-dayspring-from-on-high.text: Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace

john-epistle-god-is-light.text: This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin

john-burning-and-shining-light.text: He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light

genesis-two-great-lights.text: And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also. And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth, And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good

philippians-shine-as-lights.text: Do all things without murmurings and disputings: That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world

john-walk-while-ye-have-the-light.text: Then Jesus said unto them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth. While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light

micah-when-i-sit-in-darkness.text: Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light unto me

ecclesiastes-light-is-sweet.text: Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun

peter-day-star-arise.text: We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts

quran-lamp-that-giveth-light.text: And as a summoner unto Allah by His permission, and as a lamp that giveth light.

quran-sun-a-splendour.text: He it is Who appointed the sun a splendour and the moon a light, and measured for her stages, that ye might know the number of the years, and the reckoning. Allah created not (all) that save in truth. He detaileth the revelations for people who have knowledge.

quran-light-and-a-plain-scripture.text: O People of the Scripture! Now hath Our messenger come unto you, expounding unto you much of that which ye used to hide in the Scripture, and forgiving much. now hath come unto you light from Allah and plain Scripture,

quran-by-the-sun-and-his-brightness.text: By the sun and his brightness, And the moon when she followeth him, And the day when it revealeth him, And the night when it enshroudeth him

shakespeare-full-many-a-glorious-morning.text: Even so my sun one early morn did shine / With all triumphant splendor on my brow; / But out, alack! he was but one hour mine; / The region cloud hath mask'd him from me now. / Yet him for this my love no whit disdaineth; / Suns of the world may stain when heaven's sun staineth
shakespeare-full-many-a-glorious-morning.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-searching-eye-of-heaven.text: when the searching eye of heaven is hid, / Behind the globe, that lights the lower world, / Then thieves and robbers range abroad unseen / In murders and in outrage, boldly here; / But when from under this terrestrial ball / He fires the proud tops of the eastern pines / And darts his light through every guilty hole, / Then murders, treasons and detested sins, / The cloak of night being pluck'd from off their backs, / Stand bare and naked, trembling at themselves
shakespeare-searching-eye-of-heaven.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

francis-brother-sun.text: Praise be to Thee, my Lord, with all Thy creatures, Especially to my worshipful brother sun, The which lights up the day, and through him dost Thou brightness give; And beautiful is he and radiant with splendor great; Of Thee, most High, signification
francis-brother-sun.author: Francis of Assisi

gita-thousand-suns.text: If there should rise Suddenly within the skies Sunburst of a thousand suns Flooding earth with beams undeemed-of, Then might be that Holy One

plato-sun-is-stone.text: Do you mean that I do not believe in the godhead of the sun or moon, which is the common creed of all men? I assure you, judges, that he does not believe in them; for he says that the sun is stone, and the moon earth
plato-sun-is-stone.author: Plato

psalm-light-of-thy-countenance.text: There be many that say, Who will shew us any good? Lord, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us

peter-marvellous-light.text: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light

ephesians-children-of-light.text: For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light

acts-cloud-received-him.text: And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. And while they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel; Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven

psalm-face-to-shine.text: Turn us again, O Lord God of hosts, cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved
